t.18.1: Aṣṭāvakra said: Salutation to that tranquil light, whose very nature is bliss alone, upon whose dawning as awakened knowledge delusion becomes like a dream.
t.18.2: Having acquired all kinds of wealth, one obtains abundant enjoyments; yet without the renunciation of everything, one cannot become happy.
t.18.3: For one whose inner self has been scorched by the blazing flame of the sun of the pain of duties, where can happiness come from without a downpour of the streaming nectar of tranquility?
t.18.4: This world is mere imagination; from the standpoint of ultimate truth it is nothing at all. For those who abide in their own nature and discern both being and non-being, there is no non-being.
t.18.5: The state of the Self is not far away, nor is it gained through contraction; it is already attained, free of mental constructs, effortless, changeless and stainless.
t.18.7: All this is mere imagination; the Self is free and eternal. Having truly understood this, what does the wise one practise, like a child?
t.18.6: When mere delusion ceases, simply by grasping their own true nature, those whose sorrow has vanished shine forth, their vision free of every veil.
t.18.8: Having ascertained that the Self is Brahman and that existence and non-existence are mere imaginings, what does the one free from desire know, what does he say, and what does he do?
t.18.9: For the yogin who has become silent, having ascertained that everything is the Self, the mental constructions "This am I" and "This am I not" have dwindled away.
t.18.10: For the yogin who has become utterly tranquil, there is neither distraction nor one-pointedness, neither excess of knowledge nor dullness, neither pleasure nor pain.
t.18.11: For the yogin whose nature is free from mental constructs, there is no difference between sovereign rule and living by alms, between gain and loss, between the crowd and the forest.
t.18.12: Where is dharma, where is pleasure, where is wealth, and where is discernment for the yogin who is freed from the pairs of opposites such as 'this has been done' and 'this has not'?
t.18.13: For the yogin who is liberated while living, there is nothing whatsoever to be done, nor is there any attachment at all in his heart; here his living simply goes on as it comes.
t.18.14: Where is delusion, where indeed is the universe, where is that meditation, where is liberation, for the great-souled one who rests at the boundary of all conceptual intentions?
t.18.15: Let him by whom this universe has been seen declare, "It does not exist." But what does one free of latent desires do? Even while seeing, he does not see.
t.18.16: He by whom the supreme Brahman has been seen may think, "I am Brahman." But what does he think, the one who is free of thought and sees no second?
t.18.17: He who has seen distraction in his own self practices restraint of the mind; but the noble one is not distracted, and since there is nothing to be accomplished, what is there for him to do?
t.18.18: The wise one, though living like ordinary people, is the very opposite of the world; he sees in himself neither concentration nor distraction nor any taint.
t.18.19: The wise one who is free from both being and non-being, content and without desires, does nothing at all, even though in the eyes of the world he appears to act.
t.18.20: Whether in activity or in withdrawal from it, the wise one has no stubborn attachment. Whenever something comes to be done, he does it and abides in happiness.
t.18.21: Free of latent desires, without support, acting by his own free will, his bonds released, he moves about like a dry leaf, driven by the wind of past impressions.
t.18.22: For one who is free from saṃsāra there is never any elation, nor any dejection. Ever cool of mind, he shines like one without a body.
t.18.23: For the steadfast one who delights in the Self, whose being is cool and exceedingly pure, there is no desire to abandon anything anywhere, nor is there any loss anywhere at all.
t.18.24: The steady sage, whose mind is empty by nature and who acts spontaneously, as an ordinary person does, knows neither honor nor dishonor.
t.18.25: "This action was done by the body, not by me, whose nature is pure": he who conforms to this thought, even while acting, does not act.
t.18.26: He acts like one who does not speak of That, yet he is no fool. Liberated while living, happy and glorious, he shines even while moving through saṃsāra.
t.18.27: Thoroughly wearied by manifold deliberations, the steadfast sage has come to rest; he does not imagine, does not know, does not hear, does not see.
t.18.28: Free from both meditative absorption and distraction, the great-souled one is neither a seeker of liberation nor its opposite. Having ascertained that everything is imagined and seeing only brahman, he simply abides.
t.18.29: He within whom there is egoism acts even when he does not act; but by the steadfast one free of egoism, nothing is either done or left undone.
t.18.30: The mind of the liberated one shines forth, neither agitated nor elated, free from doership and devoid of all movement, without desire and with all doubts gone.
t.18.31: Since the mind does not set out to meditate or to act, it is without any motive; yet it still meditates and acts.
t.18.33: One-pointedness or the cessation of the mind is intensely practiced by the deluded; the wise, abiding in their own state like one asleep, see nothing that remains to be done.
t.18.32: Hearing the truth as it really is, the dull-witted man falls into bewilderment; or else some rare one, though not deluded, withdraws into himself as if he were a fool.
t.18.34: Whether by effort or without effort, the deluded one does not attain peace; the wise one becomes at peace merely through firm ascertainment of the truth.
t.18.35: Those people who are devoted to practice do not know that Self, which is pure, awakened, beloved, full, free from the world of appearances, and untouched by affliction.
t.18.36: The deluded one does not attain liberation through action in the form of practice; the blessed one, by mere knowledge, stands liberated and unchanging.
t.18.37: The deluded one does not attain that Brahman, precisely because he desires to become it; but the wise one, even without desiring it, partakes of the very nature of the supreme Brahman.
t.18.38: Without any support and agitated by their grasping, the deluded keep nourishing saṃsāra. But the wise have cut away the very root of this root of all misfortune.
t.18.39: The deluded one does not attain peace, because he wishes to become calm. The wise one, having ascertained the truth, is always tranquil of mind.
t.18.40: How can there be a vision of the Self for one who clings to what is seen? The wise do not see this or that; they see the imperishable Self.
t.18.41: Where is cessation of the mind for the deluded one who strives for it by force? For the wise one who delights in the Self alone, that cessation is always natural and unforced.
t.18.43: The dull-witted contemplate the Self as pure and non-dual, but out of delusion they do not truly know it, and so they remain without peace for as long as they live.
t.18.42: One person dwells on the idea of existence, another dwells on the idea that nothing exists; but the one who dwells on neither remains, just as he is, free from agitation.
t.18.44: The mind of one who seeks liberation does not exist without a support. The mind of the liberated one is ever free of support and free of desire.
t.18.45: Seeing the tigers of the sense-objects, the frightened ones, seeking refuge, at once enter the cave to attain cessation of thought and one-pointed concentration.
t.18.47: Free from doubt, his mind steadfast, he does not take up any practice aimed at liberation; seeing, hearing, touching, smelling and eating, he lives as he pleases, at ease.
t.18.46: Seeing the lion who is free of desires, the elephants of sense-objects quietly flee, or, if they cannot, they stay and serve him like fawning flatterers.
t.18.48: By merely hearing of the Reality, one whose understanding is pure and who is free from agitation sees neither right conduct nor wrong conduct, nor even indifference.
t.18.49: Whatever comes to be done, whenever it arises, the guileless one simply does it, be it good or bad; for his actions are like those of a child.
t.18.50: Through freedom one attains happiness; through freedom one gains the Supreme. Through freedom one may reach perfect peace; through freedom, the highest state.
t.18.51: When one recognizes non-doership and non-enjoyership as belonging to one's own Self, then all the modifications of the mind are indeed exhausted.
t.18.52: The state of the wise one, though unrestrained and free of contrivance, shines forth; but not so the artificial calm of the deluded one whose mind is full of desire.
t.18.53: The wise, who have cast off all mental constructions, unbound and with minds set free, sometimes revel amid great enjoyments and sometimes enter the caves of the mountains.
t.18.55: Even when mocked and reviled by servants, sons, wives, grandsons, and kinsmen, the yogī is not disturbed in the least.
t.18.54: Even on seeing and honoring a learned Vedic scholar, a deity, a holy place of pilgrimage, a woman, a king, or a beloved friend, no lingering desire whatsoever arises in the heart of the steadfast sage.
t.18.56: Though content, he is not content; though distressed, he is not distressed. Only those who are like him know that wondrous state of his, each and every phase of it.
t.18.57: The sense that something must be done is itself saṃsāra. The wise do not see it, for they are empty in form, formless, changeless and free from all affliction.
t.18.58: The deluded one, even while doing nothing, is restless everywhere out of agitation; but the skilled one, even while performing his duties, remains undisturbed.
t.18.59: Happily he sits, happily he sleeps, happily he comes and goes; happily he speaks, happily he eats: even in the midst of worldly affairs, he whose mind is at peace remains at ease.
t.18.60: He who, though acting in the world like an ordinary person, by his very nature feels no distress at all, shines forth free from afflictions, unagitated like a vast lake.
t.18.61: Even the withdrawal of the deluded turns into activity, while even the activity of the wise one bears the fruit of withdrawal.
t.18.62: Aversion to possessions is mostly seen in the deluded one. For one whose desires have melted away, even regarding the body, where is attachment, where is detachment?
t.18.63: The vision of the deluded is always attached to meditation and non-meditation; but for one established in the Self, that same vision, even while meditating on what is to be meditated upon, takes the form of non-seeing.
t.18.64: The sage who, free of desire in all undertakings, moves about like a child, is pure; for him there is no taint even when action is being performed.
t.18.65: Blessed indeed is that knower of the Self who remains even-minded toward all things, whose mind is free of craving while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, and eating.
t.18.66: Where is worldly existence, where is mere appearance, where is the goal and where the means to it, for the wise one who, like space, is ever free of all mental constructs?
t.18.67: Victorious is he who has renounced all aims, whose very form is the fullness of his own innate bliss, and whose spontaneous, uncontrived samādhi abides in the unbounded.
t.18.68: What is the use of saying much here? The great-souled one who has known the truth, free of longing for both enjoyment and liberation, is always and everywhere without attachment.
t.18.69: Having abandoned the duality of the world, beginning with mahat, which is a mere unfolding of names, what duty remains for one whose awareness is pure?
t.18.70: He who is firmly convinced that all this is mere illusion and that nothing truly exists, whose radiance is imperceptible and who is pure, becomes tranquil by his very nature.
t.18.71: For one whose nature is pure radiance and who does not see any objective existence, where is injunction, where is dispassion, where is renunciation, or where even is tranquility?
t.18.72: For one who shines forth in infinite form and does not perceive Prakṛti, where is bondage, or where is liberation? Where is joy, where is sorrow?
t.18.73: In this world of transmigration, which extends only as far as the intellect, it is mere illusion that unfolds. The wise one, free from the sense of 'mine', free from ego, and free from desire, shines forth.
t.18.74: For the sage who sees the Self as imperishable and free from all torment, where is knowledge, and where is the universe? Where is the body, or the thought of "I" and "mine"?
t.18.76: The dull-witted one, even after hearing that Reality, does not abandon his delusion; through outward effort he appears free of mental constructs, but inwardly he still craves the objects of the senses.
t.18.75: If the dull-witted man gives up practices such as restraint of the mind, he at once falls to making wishes and idle chatter from that very moment.
t.18.77: He whose actions have fallen away through knowledge, though in the eyes of the world he is a doer of deeds, finds no occasion to do or even to say anything at all.
t.18.78: For the steadfast one who is ever changeless and free from fear, where is darkness, where is light, and where is loss? For him there is nothing whatsoever.
t.18.79: Where is fortitude, where is discernment, or where even fearlessness, for the yogin whose own nature is beyond words and who is without any individual nature?
t.18.81: He does not long for gain at all, nor does he grieve over loss; the cool mind of the steadfast one is filled with nectar itself.
t.18.80: There is no heaven, nor indeed any hell, nor even liberation while living. What is the use of saying much here? In the vision of yoga, there is nothing at all.
t.18.82: Free from desire, he does not praise the peaceful one, nor does he blame even the wicked. Equal in sorrow and joy and content, he sees nothing whatsoever that must be done.
t.18.83: The steadfast one neither hates worldly existence nor longs to behold the Self. Freed from joy and anger, he is neither dead nor does he live.
t.18.84: Without attachment to sons, wife and the like, without desire for the objects of the senses, free of concern even for his own body, and free of hope, the wise one shines.
t.18.85: Contentment is everywhere for the steadfast one who lives on whatever comes his way, who wanders the lands at his own free will, and who lies down to sleep wherever the sun happens to set.
t.18.86: Let the body fall or let it rise; the great-souled one has no concern for it, for, resting in the ground of his own true nature, he has forgotten the whole of worldly existence.
t.18.87: Possessing nothing, moving as he pleases, free from the pairs of opposites, his doubts cut away, unattached to all things, the wise one rejoices, alone.
t.18.88: Free from all sense of 'mine', the steadfast sage shines forth, regarding a clod of earth, a stone and gold as equal; the knot of his heart has been cut clean through, and rajas and tamas have been shaken off.
t.18.89: In the heart of one who is unconcerned with everything, there are no latent desires whatsoever. With whom can such a liberated, fully contented soul be compared?
t.18.90: Though knowing, he does not know; though seeing, he does not see; though speaking, he does not speak. Who else but the one free from desires can be like this?
t.18.91: Whether a mendicant or a king, he who is free from desire shines forth, he whose notion of things as good or bad has fallen away.
t.18.92: Where is self-will, where is restraint, or where is the ascertainment of truth for the yogin who has become guileless straightforwardness itself and whose purpose has been fulfilled?
t.18.93: What is inwardly experienced by one who is content through resting in the Self, free of desire, his sorrow gone, how can that be told, and to whom?
t.18.94: Though asleep, he is not in deep sleep; though lying in dream, he does not dream; though in waking, he is not awake: the wise one is content at every step.
t.18.95: The wise one, though having thoughts, is free from thought; though having senses, is without senses; though endowed with intellect, is without intellect; though having an ego, is free from ego.
t.18.96: He is neither happy nor unhappy, neither detached nor attached, neither seeking liberation nor liberated; he is neither something nor anything at all.
t.18.97: Even in distraction he is not distracted; in meditative absorption he is not one who possesses absorption; even in dullness he is not dull; even in learning he is not learned: blessed is he.
t.18.98: The liberated one, at ease in whatever state he finds himself, content in having done what was to be done, and equal everywhere, through freedom from craving does not recall what he has done or left undone.
t.18.99: Being praised, he is not pleased; being blamed, he does not become angry. He is not at all disturbed by death, nor does he rejoice in life.
t.18.100: The one whose mind is wholly at peace runs neither toward the crowded haunts of men nor toward the forest; however things may be and wherever he is, he abides ever the same.
